title: Dont Tell People They Are Wrong - Tell Them How Right You Are Instead
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note argues against a common persuasion habit: explicitly telling someone their idea is wrong before offering a better one. The author contends this creates defensiveness that outlasts the conversation and actually blocks people from hearing the improved answer. The alternative is to skip the labeling step entirely and move straight to articulating your own view -- phrases like 'let me tell you what I believe' replace 'you're wrong.' The piece closes with a self-audit challenge: count how often you tell people they're wrong in a week, since many leaders do it more than they realize.
points: Telling someone they are wrong triggers defensiveness that outlasts the conversation and blocks persuasion.
The recommended alternative is skipping the 'you're wrong' framing and moving straight to your own view.
Sample phrasing is offered: 'Interesting suggestion, let me tell you what I believe.'
Leaders are urged to audit how often they correct or negate others before offering an alternative.
The piece frames this as an old, ingrained habit rather than a deliberate persuasion strategy.
quotes: The fact is, no one likes to be told they are wrong. Once told they are wrong, people stop listening and get defensive about their views.
The shock, dismay, or offense of being told they are wrong lasts beyond the initial negative reaction.
The better choice is to avoid ever labeling what others think or conclude as wrong, and instead simply emphasize how right you are.

Interesting suggestion, let me tell you what I believe…” or “I haven’t thought of that, but let me tell you what I have thought of…” are examples of not calling out what is wrong but instead moving quickly to what you believe is right.
The better habit is to give up telling others they don’t get it and to focus on what you believe is right.
Everyone is wrong now and again, but good leaders don’t rub it in.
